items.title: Bibliotheken en scholen kunnen bordspel CODER.IO aanvragen voor programmeren zonder scherm
items.raw_text: Bibliotheken die met scholen samenwerken, schoolbibliotheken en mediatheken kunnen tot en met 30 november kosteloos het bordspel CODER.IO aanvragen. Met het spel leren leerlingen vanaf 10 jaar programmeren zonder scherm. OCLC geeft twaalf exemplaren cadeau aan de Bibliotheek op school, ter ere van twee jubilea: Jeugdbieb.nl bestaat 25 jaar en productanalist Marcel Wijngaard werkt dit jaar 25 jaar bij OCLC. Zijn kinderen bedachten het spel. Wijngaards zoon Edwin programmeert al sinds zijn zesde. Toen hij als tienjarige minder op zijn scherm mocht, ging hij aan de keukentafel verder met post-its, getekende kaartjes en zelfgemaakte poppetjes. Samen met zijn zus Anna werkte hij het idee in tweeënhalf jaar uit tot een bordspel. In 2025 brachten ze het uit bij hun eigen uitgeverij Vinea Games. Hoe CODER.IO werkt In CODER.IO zijn spelers een robot die via een portaal terug naar huis wil. De route leggen ze met codekaarten, zoals vooruit, draaien en springen. Loopt de robot vast, dan zoeken de spelers de fout en verbeteren ze hun code. In latere levels komen herhalingen en als-dan-opdrachten erbij. items.title: Statement from the IFLA Governing Board on SIGL and communications from IFLA Members
items.raw_text: The IFLA Governing Board notes the recent correspondence on IFLA-L concerning SIGL and regrets that matters have reached this point. At the same time, we recognise the concerns raised by members, particularly regarding the level of expenditure incurred by SIGL, given its current governance structure of three Board members and one adviser. IFLA has separately been undertaking its own due diligence in relation to these matters. In the interests of transparency, we would welcome SIGL making its full audit report for 2025 available. We would also welcome greater clarity regarding the role of its adviser, Mr Gerald Leitner, including the scope of the role, remuneration and contractual terms. We also regret that SIGL did not take forward the suggestion that former IFLA President Vicki McDonald join its Board. We believe that such an appointment would have provided an important and constructive demonstration of openness and transparency, as well as helping to rebuild confidence. Our overriding priority is to ensure that the Legacy Grant is used for its intended purpose: to strengthen the global library field . We remain committed to ensuring that concerns about its governance and use are addressed transparently, factually and in the interests of IFLA and its members. items.title: Quoting Prompting Claude Fable 5.2
items.raw_text: Claude Fable 5.2 responds closely to what the prompt says about who owns the code it works on. In Anthropic’s testing on small coding tasks, when a prompt said nothing about ownership or presented the code base as someone else’s, the model tended to add to the existing structure, even when that repeated existing code. [...] If you want the model to improve the structure as it works, say that the code is its own: This codebase is yours: what it's for and how it's built are your call, and you'll keep building on it. In Anthropic’s testing on small coding tasks, the model merged repeated code in about half of the tries with this sentence, and in under a tenth of the tries without it. — Prompting Claude Fable 5.2 , Anthropic documentation Tags: prompt-engineering , anthropic , generative-ai , ai , llms , claude-mythos-fable

items.title: Locating the source of a mysterious beep with Claude
items.raw_text: Our house has a box room, full of boxes that we still haven't unpacked from our last move. A couple of weeks ago something in that room started intermittently beeping . The beeps were far enough apart that standing in the room and trying to determine the source of the noise was frustrating, and I really didn't want to dig through every one of those boxes. So I had Claude Code build Beep Locator , a software system for triangulating the source of a mysterious beep using multiple devices scattered around the room. Here's what Beep Locator looks like after it has been running for a while: You run Python web server to show the primary UI, and then use the QR code or URL to connect as many devices as you can spare to act as listeners - I was using two iPads, a phone, a MacBook Pro and a Surface Ultra. The devices then play noises to each other to help estimate their locations. This didn't work particularly well, so I added a "Rough mode" where you can drag their icons around in the space to provide rough locations which are then adjusted based on those sounds. Once that's set up, the devices all listen for the beep! I added a clapping mode too so I could test it by clapping my hands in different locations around the room - displayed as diamonds on the map. This helped me gain confidence that it was capable of locating a sound. Beeps show up on the map as an X, plus a line in the "Sounds located" log. items.raw_text: This story originally appeared in The Algorithm, our weekly newsletter on AI. To get stories like this in your inbox first, sign up here . As voters went to the polls across the US last week, I was in Ashburn, Virginia, part of what’s known as Data Center Alley—the world’s largest data center hub. It’s also where the backlash now sweeping the country arguably first began taking shape. Driving through it is surreal. Concrete monolithic buildings loom along every major road, with names like Skybox and CloudHQ. It’s accepted wisdom in Big Tech that the war against data centers must be about something bigger than just data centers themselves. Two days after the midterms, OpenAI’s chief global affairs officer, Chris Lehane, wrote that data centers “have become a proxy for public unease about affordability, corporate power, and people losing control over their futures.” It’s a culture war, in other words. But spending a few days in Data Center Alley left me wondering if it’s really the proxy that Lehane describes. I came away convinced that the data center backlash is more about electricity than Big Tech admits. The industry can improve its image, but it can’t escape the physical consequences of its enormous appetite for electricity. Here’s why. items.title: Nancy Pelosi’s replacement is ready to regulate AI
items.raw_text: As a California state senator, Scott Wiener authored legislation aimed at curbing the risks of advanced AI. Now, after winning a tight congressional race for former Speaker of the House Nancy Pelosi’s open San Francisco seat, he could play a key role in setting federal AI policy. I spoke with Wiener on Friday, only a few hours after he had been declared the victor. But he was already thinking about AI risk. The previous day, the AI nonprofit METR had released a report that had been widely interpreted as evidence that Anthropic had achieved recursive self-improvement, a phenomenon in which AI meaningfully contributes to its own advancement and AI progress potentially spins out of control. “It’s very concerning,” Wiener said, citing the report as evidence that we are quickly running out of time to regulate AI. “It was my hope that Congress would take decisive action before [the end of] this year,” he said. “That does not appear to be happening.” Wiener has been increasingly focused on AI in recent years, and he’s made many of the AI safety movement’s concerns his own: During our 20-minute conversation, he used the phrase “recursive self-improvement” half a dozen times, for example.“We need to slow this down,” he says. “Because it’s moving very quickly, and we could sleepwalk into a disaster.” Wiener has already had real influence on AI policy. items.title: Claude Code is accidentally exposing secrets all over GitHub
items.raw_text: Claude Code is leaking sensitive information on public GitHub instances thanks to a partial oversight in the way its settings files are handled. That's the finding of AI security researchers at Apiiro, who discovered thousands of secrets , including database passwords, API tokens, and root logins, amid Claude Code settings files embedded in GitHub repositories. The leak stems from the way Claude Code handles user approval for automated shell commands. When a user chooses the "Yes, and don't ask again" option to approve running a command, that choice gets stored as part of a rule in the local ".claude/settings.local.json" file on the user's computer. That rule is sometimes coded as a pattern, but the command itself is often written to that settings file as is, including any sensitive information that may be embedded within it. This isn't really a significant security issue if the settings file stays on the user's local machine (assuming that machine doesn't become compromised itself, of course). And Anthropic notes in its Claude Code documentation that this particular settings file gets added to the developer's global .gitignore list , which usually prevents it from being shared publicly.
